title: Tech Stocks Tumble as Investors Ask AI Spending to Prove Itself
summary: Friday, October 30, 2026, was a rough day for many big technology stocks. Investors grew worried that excitement about artificial intelligence, or AI, had pushed some stock prices too high. A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, and its price can rise or fall as people decide what they think the company is worth. The S&P 500, a broad list of large American companies, fell about 1.8 percent. That was its worst single day since June. The Nasdaq, which includes many technology companies, dropped 2.9 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.1 percent. In Canada, the main S&P/TSX index closed down 1.7 percent after falling as much as 2.3 percent during the afternoon. Chipmaker Intel led the slide, falling 28.6 percent, its worst drop since 1974. Intel had reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but its forecast for profit in the final three months of the year was lower than analysts expected. Chief executive Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. Amazon fell 1.4 percent after reporting weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected, and it reported spending heavily on property and equipment, mainly for AI investments. The day before, Alphabet, the company behind Google and YouTube, had dropped more than 12 percent after saying it spent more cash during the summer than in the spring, also largely on AI. Portfolio manager Joe Tigay said investors are moving out of the hopes and dreams phase and into the show me phase, meaning they now want clearer proof that the spending will pay off. Not every stock fell. ExxonMobil rose 2.2 percent and Chevron added 1.8 percent after both oil companies reported stronger summer profit than analysts expected.
why_it_matters: The sharp falls show how much confidence in AI spending matters to the wider market: when investors doubt that the spending will pay off, even large technology companies can lose value quickly.

background_read: A stock market index is a list that tracks how a group of companies' shares are doing, so when many big technology companies fall, the indexes that include them fall too.
Artificial intelligence systems need powerful computer chips and large data centers, and companies spend heavily to build them in hopes that customers will later pay for AI tools and services.

Investors buy shares based on what they think a company will earn in the future, so when a company's profit outlook is weaker than expected, or its spending looks larger than the payoff so far, they may sell its shares and its price drops.
That selling can spread across technology shares when investors start to question whether earlier excitement about artificial intelligence had pushed prices higher than current earnings can support.
